Copper Quarterly July 2010 

# Executive Summary All scrapped out 



- The global copper markets remain tight for concentrates, scrap and cathode.  The return of seasonally stronger growth in North America and Europe in Q2 resulted in slightly stronger **consumption in the World ex-China** .  As a result, Q2 saw the first quarterly deficit since 2008 in the cathode market, despite stronger than expected production. 



- We have revised our estimates of **Chinese copper consumption** growth since 2009 due to higher semis production than previously estimated.  This higher total copper demand is being met by cathode, as **scrap** remains tight globally, with Chinese scrap imports still more than 30% below H1 2008 peak levels.  Chinese domestic scrap generation is growing, but this is not enough to close the import gap. 



- **Mine production** has seen relatively low levels of disruption so far this year and we have reduced our disruption allowance in 2010 and 2011.  As a result, slightly higher committed mine production will see **refined output** rise by 2% this year and by 5% in 2011. 



- With exchange stocks being drawn down by a combination of the deficit in Q2 and modest restocking, **prices** will remain supported in volatile trading through Q3.  In Q4, we expect prices to pick up as the surplus recorded in Q3 narrows and in anticipation of a deficit in H1 2011.  We expect prices to rise towards $8,000/t (~$3.60/lb) in the first half of 2011. 



- In 2012, we forecast rising consumption on the back of continued economic recovery, which will be matched by production growth as more projects come on stream, leading to a balanced market.  Thereafter, refined production will lag that of consumption, as the latter is driven higher in part by the legacy of the structural scrap shortage from the 2008-2009 downturn. 



- We would anticipate increased investment money shifting into copper ahead of the **growing deficits in 2013-2014** .  This will see prices average $8,200/t (~$3.70/lb) in 2013, and scaling higher to $8,800/t (~$4.00/lb) by 2014.  As a result, these high prices will lead to further substitution, as the semis industry focuses on higher value added refined applications (mainly electrical).

A combination of slightly higher mine output and scrap usage by smelters and refineries boosts refined output in later years. **Prices** : $250/t less in 2010; $300/t higher in 2011 and up by an average $550/t in 2012-2014. ## 2010: a year of consolidation Copper prices entered 2010 on a high and tested $8,000/t ($3.60/lb) in early April, but then went on to succumb to wider fears of the sustainability of the economic recovery and the pace of Chinese economic growth. This downward trajectory in the price came despite the return of the usual Q2 seasonal upturn in demand, and the appearance of a market deficit for the first time since the financial crisis hit two years ago. Exchange stocks have seen a steady drawn down over and above the Q2 deficit. This disconnect from the current fundamentals is not surprising. Chinese buying in Q2 2009, due primarily to scrap replacement, pulled forward the upturn in prices to last year. This then prompted financial investors to re-enter the market ahead of the perceived economic recovery. As a result, cathode output in H1 2010 was up by an estimated 6.7% year-on-year on the same period in 2009. This reflects the weak outturn in refined production due to the collapse of available scrap last year and sulphuric acid related cutbacks. However, we estimate that cathode production in the second half of this year will be lower on a year-on-year basis, as smelter and refinery maintenance shutdowns increase and comparison is made with accelerating production growth throughout H2 2009. On balance, even with the increase in mine output, concentrate availability remains a constraint on refined output. We have re-estimated Chinese semis production growth from 2005. Over the period 20052008, we believe that the difference from our previous forecasts was met by higher scrap usage; therefore, our refined consumption figures remain unchanged. In 2009, however, given the dearth of scrap in China, we estimate that cathode accounted for a higher proportion of consumption in the semis industry. Hence, our Chinese refined consumption growth for last year is now 26% instead of 23% in our April Quarterly. Although Chinese consumption growth will moderate in H2, the lags from the stimulus spending and credit expansion should support semis growth and refined consumption through the balance of 2010. The scrap replacement effect from our increase in overall semis production growth this year has also led us to increase our 2010 estimate of refined consumption growth to 13%. As a result of these revisions, our estimate of the stock build in China in 2009 has been reduced, and particularly that attributed to speculative players. Further research indicates that most of the speculative stock build last year resulte

d from the easy credit conditions that allowed speculators to jump on the copper bandwagon. As most speculative players holding copper bought last year are currently sitting on paper profits, they have little incentive to release the material. Indeed, we believe that there has been only 50-100,000t of the speculative stock drawn down so far this year. The likely trigger would be the inability to roll over any loan that had been taken out to buy copper as a speculative investment. Chinese scrap imports on a gross weight basis are curre

ntly still 37% below peak H1 2008 levels.  Domestic generation has not been able to make up the difference, leaving scrap availability very tight in China.  Despite some talk of an increase in the copper content of scrap imports which would boost the copper contained in the material entering China, refined imports of cathode remain elevated and smelters are struggling to find concentrates.  This is leaving new smelters starved of raw material, resulting in record low TC/RCs for concentrates, as well as delays to several smelter expansions in China. 

The rest of Asia is continuing to maintain growth following its V-shaped recovery in copper consumption last year and into 2010.  North America and Europe saw a return of typical seasonally stronger consumption in Q2.  Given the latest economic data releases, there are some doubts about the sustainability of demand growth in H2, but we forecast that these wobbles in sentiment will not lead to a double dip recession. 

Stronger Chinese growth from a higher 2009 base, plus a slight increase in consumption in other regions, means our estimate for global consumption in 2010 is 300,000t higher than in the April Quarterly.  In the second half, we see demand growth moderating, resulting in a modest surplus over the balance of the year.  However, we do not see this surplus translating into rising exchange stocks.  So far stocks on the LME have accounted for the bulk of the 160,000t drop in exchange stocks since the peak in February.  Furthermore, the level of cancelled warrants indicates that LME stocks are currently on course to be run down to the lows hit last year during the peak of the Chinese import boom.  The small market deficit in Q2 accounts for only some of this drawdown.  We believe the rest of the drawdown is due to a combination of factors: rising Chinese imports and some marginal restocking.  Chinese imports are likely to increase monthon-month in at least July, given that the SHFE/LME arbitrage window has been open on a cash basis since May.  In addition, we believe there will be further marginal restocking, as consumers

and merchants have started to believe that the worst of the recession is over and the increase in end-use orders will be sustained. 

We estimate that prices will hit their nadir on a quarterly average basis for the year in volatile trading conditions in Q3, as demand moderates.  In Q4, demand will begin to outpace the growth in production and the surplus will narrow compared to Q3.  In addition, we expect that the jitters over the sustainability of the economic recovery will fade and financial investors will eye a tightening copper market in H1 2011.  As a result, we expect prices to be bid back up above $7,000/t (~$3.20/lb) in the final quarter of the year.  All in all, 2010 is shaping up to be a year of consolidation of the price gains since the depths of the financial crisis in

Q4 2008. 

## Balanced market in 2011-2012 and… 

In 2011, as the economic recovery becomes more entrenched in the industrialised world, demand is forecast to continue to recover from the 2009 lows.  Scrap growth, however, will remain constrained until the largest generator of old scrap, the construction sector, recovers in the industrialised world.  We do not forecast this occurring until late 2011.  Therefore, semis producers will be forced to consume proportionately more cathode until then. 

We expect that supply disruptions will remain at a relatively low level and have therefore reduced our mine production disruption allowance for 2011 by a percentage point to 6.5%, which raises mine output by 175,000t.  New greenfield projects and the ramping up of projects from earlier years will help boost total mine output by 4% next year.  However, we expect to see refined output rise by 5%, as smelters win the battle for scrap against semi fabricators.   All told, refined output is forecast to rise by almost 1Mt in the year, but this will be matched by a similar rise in consumption, leaving the market balanced in 2011. 

As for prices, we expect sentiment to pick up in H1 2011 as the market moves into the seasonal deficit in Q2 and fears over the sustainability of the recovery fade.  We therefore expect prices to bounce towards $8,000/t ($3.60) in Q2, as consumers outbid each other for

Despite a surplus in H2 offsetting the deficit in H1, prices should remain supported, with average prices for 2011 as a whole at $7,700/t ($3.50/lb). In 2012, the market is forecast to be broadly balanced as production growth, due to increasing tonnages from projects, offsets the rise in demand on the back of the economic recovery. However, prices are expected to rise more than the immediate fundamentals justify, as financial investors bid up prices ahead of a move into structural deficits in 2013 and 2014. ## … dearth of scrap leading to … A major constraining factor on both copper production and consumption growth will be the lack of scrap. The collapse in scrap availability in 2008-2009 means we have lost almost five years worth of growth in the scrap market (see chart on page 7). Scrap trade can be used as a proxy for overall scrap availability. It will take until 2014 to regain the level of scrap traded in the world in 2008 on a high projection, using the trend rate of growth from 2001-2008. On a lower projection, using a more realistic growth rate of that based on the trend between June 200

9 and May 2010, it would take another two years (to 2016) to regain peak levels. Scrap generation can by its very nature only be boosted by a combination of: Increased levels of scrapping of copper containing products; - Increased capture of the copper contained in scrapped products and/or demolished buildings; Increased demolition of buildings. It is important to recall that the sharp increase in scrap exported to China in the 2004-2008 period was fed by the running down of scrap stockpiles. We do not believe that there are any significant volumes of material waiting to be released to the market. Therefore, scrap availability will be limited to the factors noted above. In the short term, the end of the wave of stimulus related vehicle scrappage schemes will lead to declining scrap availability from this end-use. However, we anticipate that the higher prices further out, combined with increasing environmental awareness and legislation, will boost the pace of recycling as exampled by Boliden’s increase in capacity to process electronic scrap. The copper released from the demolition of smaller, unmodernised buildings in China and the other growth markets will release only modest quantities compared to the copper required by their replacements. Increased theft is only likely to increase substitution, such as the replacement of copper telecom cable with fibre optic cables. ## … deepening deficits in 2013-14 and $4/lb copper by 2014 Mined production growth in the medium term will suffer constraints through lack of personnel and mining equipment availability, as experienced in the booming 2006-2008 period. In order for refined production to grow faster than mine output, we believe direct use of scrap by semi-fabricators (mainly in brass mill products) will decline and that this scrap will be diverted to smelters and

refineries.  This increase in refined output, though, will not raise the overall copper units available to the market and we expect deficits to emerge, widening to over 350,000t by 2014.  As stock-to-consumption ratios fall to below the lows reached in 2007 and the fundamental tightness asserts itself, we expect to see prices rise to an annual average of about $8,800/t ($4.00/lb) by 2014.  In such an environment of tightening structural fundamentals, speculation and investment will inevitably be attracted back to a ‘tight’ LME market in an effort to earn superior returns to those on offer through broader financial vehicles. In addition, these high prices will lead to further substitution, as the semis industry focuses on higher value added refined applications (mainly electrical).  In this case, even market segments that had previously been immune will be drawn into the substitution net.

## Points to watch 



- In our scenario driven by the upside macroeconomic alternative case in Appendix A we have assumed a steady improvement in demand in H2 2010 compared with the first part of the year. Chinese demand is also predicted to surprise on the upside in 2011.  This higher consumption outlook is combined with a tight scrap market, while mine production remains unchanged from our base case as the supply response to higher prices is already in the forecast.  This would result in a narrowing of the surplus in 2010 and a substantial 2011 market deficit.  The average LME 3-month price for next year under this scenario is $8,400/t.  The short term upside surprise is followed by a tightening by the Chinese authorities, and the market narrows back towards balance by 2013.  However, with stocks down to critical levels, prices are still high and edge up towards $9,300/t by 2014. 



- In our downside scenario, again driven by the downside macroeconomic alternative scenario, we have assumed a further slowdown in activity in H2 2010 from the negative effects of the spending cuts various governments have announced to rein in their deficits and contagion from debt restructuring in Europe.  In this case global consumption in 2011 would be 3% less than in our base case and would lead to project delays and some mine cutbacks denting the market surplus next year.  As reported stocks rise above 1.8Mt, we forecast LME 3- month prices would dip below $6,000/t in 2011.  A cyclical economic recovery through 2014 would see prices scale back up towards $8,000/t by the end of the period. 



- Outside of the scenarios outlined above, mine underperformance will generally provide support for prices, as will the high floor of mine costs.  We have factored in a lower mine disruption allowance in 2010 and 2011 of 3.1% and 6.5%, respectively.  However, if in reality it turns out that disruptions next year are on the high side, then mine output would be almost 1Mt less than forecast bas

ed on a 12% allowance.  This allowance is calculated from the average disruption recorded in 2002, 2005, 2006, 2007 and 2008, the most recent years with high levels of disruption.  A disruption allowance mid-way between the two of about 9% would, on its own, lead to a shift into deficit and higher prices similar to that in the upside scenario outlined above. 



- Economisation and substitution, driven by the record gap between copper prices and those of competing materials (especially aluminium), is here to stay.  A copper price rising towards $8,000/t next year and a price ratio to aluminium of 3.8 (as implied in our base case) could bring forward substitution more quickly than we have factored in.  This would result in lower consumption, a consequently looser market and lower prices. 



- Should any of the above lead to prices falling, we anticipate the SRB would come back into the market to replenish stocks further, thus limiting the downside to any price correction. 



- A combination of consumption outperforming and supply underperforming would be highly supportive for copper prices under any short, medium or long term scenarios.
